stories.headline: Air India to Test All Pilots for Banned Substances After Marijuana Incident
stories.summary:
Air India announced Thursday it will immediately test all of its pilots for banned substances, following an incident last week in which a Phuket-to-Delhi flight suddenly lost altitude and a preliminary report indicated the senior pilot had to retake a substance test after reportedly testing positive for marijuana. Seventeen passengers and crew were injured when the Airbus dropped approximately 91 meters (300 feet) shortly after departure on August 4. Both pilots have been removed from duties pending investigation by Indian authorities, Airbus, and France's air safety agency.

The new testing regime goes beyond existing regulatory requirements, which mandate that at least 10 percent of pilots be tested at random. Pilots at Air India's budget arm, Air India Express, are also subject to the expanded testing starting Thursday. Tests will cover both banned substances and medications prohibited under aviation regulations, and will be conducted alongside training sessions at Air India's academy and other locations.

The announcement comes as Air India remains under intense scrutiny following a June 2025 crash of a flight from Ahmedabad to London that killed 241 people on board and 19 on the ground — one of the deadliest aviation disasters in recent years. The airline, which recently appointed former Ethiopian Airlines boss Tewolde Gebremariam as its new chief executive, stated it was 'important to go further' than regulatory minimums to uphold 'the highest standards of safety and professionalism.'

stories.headline: NTSB: Engine Fan Blade Failure Caused Ryanair Window Blowout That Sucked Passenger Partially Out of Plane
stories.summary:
U.S. investigators have released a preliminary report concluding that a broken engine fan blade caused a Ryanair cabin window to shatter mid-flight last month, partially sucking a passenger's head and right shoulder out of the aircraft. The National Transportation Safety Board said the No. 2 engine on the July 10 flight from Thessaloniki, Greece, to Memmingen, Germany, suffered a fan-blade-out failure during climb, sending fragments into the fuselage. Serbian national Ljubisa Karovic was left seriously injured, and his wife and two other passengers held onto his legs for several minutes before the crew declared an emergency and returned to Thessaloniki.

The NTSB report detailed that the flight crew received a high-vibration engine alert during climb, reduced engine power, and carried out checks before vibrations resumed and a loud bang prompted an emergency descent. The engine had undergone ultrasonic inspections in May with no findings of fault. Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary had previously suggested the incident may have been caused by foreign object damage.

U.S. investigators were delegated the full investigation by Greek authorities. The incident has raised fresh questions about engine inspection protocols for the aircraft type. The plane was operated by Ryanair's subsidiary Malta Air.

stories.headline: Trump Administration Cancels Biden-Era National Interest Electric Transmission Corridor Designations
stories.summary:
The Trump administration's Energy Department announced this week it will not move forward with designating three areas as National Interest Electric Transmission Corridors — a Biden-era initiative intended to accelerate power line construction in parts of Pennsylvania, Colorado, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Nebraska, and the Dakotas. The corridor designations would have granted federal authority to streamline permitting and potentially override state-level objections to new transmission infrastructure.

Supporters of the Biden-era effort argued that expanding high-voltage transmission capacity is essential to meeting growing electricity demand driven by data centers, electric vehicles, and the broader clean energy transition. Grid analysts have warned that the U.S. faces a significant transmission bottleneck that could impede reliability and slow the integration of renewable energy sources. Critics of the federal designation process, including some states'-rights advocates and Republican officials, contended that the approach overstepped federal authority and undermined local control over land use and energy planning.

The decision is the latest in a series of Trump administration reversals of Biden-era energy and climate policies. It comes amid heightened national concern about power grid stability, illustrated by ongoing droughts and heat events straining electricity supplies across multiple regions.

stories.headline: Mali Grants Presidential Pardon to Frenchman Convicted of Plotting Coup
stories.summary:
Mali's government announced Thursday that President Assimi Goïta has granted a presidential pardon to Yann Vezilier, a French national who was sentenced to 20 years in prison after being convicted of plotting a coup against the Malian junta on behalf of French intelligence. Vezilier and a number of Malian army generals and soldiers were arrested approximately a year ago on charges of attempting to destabilize Goïta's government. The pardon is accompanied by Vezilier's immediate expulsion from Malian territory.

France's foreign ministry had previously called accusations that Vezilier was working as a French spy 'unfounded' and has not yet commented on the pardon. Mali's government stated the act of clemency 'does not call into question the facts established' by the trial, which it said respected all defense rights. The reasons behind Mali's decision to pardon Vezilier at this time remain unclear.

The episode reflects the deeply strained relationship between Mali and France. Mali, a former French colony, expelled French forces in 2022 and has since aligned more closely with Russia to combat a persistent Islamist insurgency. Goïta, who seized power in a 2021 coup, has consolidated authority further — dissolving political parties, extending his transition period until at least 2030, and naming himself defense minister after Mali's defense minister was killed in a suicide truck bombing in April.

stories.headline: Romania Shuts Only Nuclear Plant as Danube Hits 30-Year Low, Threatening European Power Supplies
stories.summary:
Romania has shut down both reactors at its Cernavodă nuclear power plant — the country's only nuclear facility — after extreme heat drove the Danube River to its lowest levels in 30 years, cutting off the water supply needed for reactor cooling. The two 706-megawatt reactors together supply roughly 20% of Romania's electricity, and plant director Romeo Urjan said a restart is not expected within the next 10 days. Engineers had attempted to maintain water flow by sinking barges loaded with rocks into the river, but the effort proved insufficient.

The shutdown is part of a broader energy and climate crisis gripping Europe. Neighboring Hungary is also at risk: its sole nuclear plant at Paks, which has four Soviet-era reactors, has faced similar Danube water-level problems. Romania's hydropower capacity — normally a backup source — has also been sharply curtailed by the same drought conditions. Coal and gas generation supplemented by imports will be needed to cover evening demand when solar and wind output falls.

The crisis extends well beyond power generation. The Rhine River is also at critically low levels, severely restricting commercial shipping traffic. Italy's largest agricultural trade group estimates climate-related damage from this summer's heatwaves, droughts, and wildfires could exceed €3 billion. France's environment minister warned that recent heatwaves could cost €10 billion to €15 billion in direct and indirect losses, and Dutch bank Triodos cautioned that the economic damage could erase most of the EU's projected growth for the year.

Scientists note that Europe is warming twice as fast as the global average, according to the EU's Copernicus climate service, making extreme heat events and associated water stress increasingly frequent. Temperatures in England provisionally reached 38.1°C (100.6°F) on Thursday at Kew Gardens, potentially a record for the date. The Romanian shutdown is only the second in Cernavodă's history — the first occurred in 2003.

stories.headline: Hegseth Calls Reports of Sailors Attempting to Jump Overboard USS Abraham Lincoln 'Completely Misrepresented'
stories.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pushed back Thursday against a wave of reports describing deteriorating conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, the aircraft carrier deployed in support of U.S. military operations related to the Iran conflict. Appearing on Newsmax, Hegseth said conditions on the ship had been 'completely misrepresented,' though he did not directly address specific allegations of supply shortages, water contamination, or declining sailor mental health.

The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea for nearly nine months in what officials describe as a record-setting deployment. Reports from multiple outlets have alleged that the grueling tour has produced a mental health crisis aboard the ship, with some sailors reportedly attempting to jump overboard. Senate Democrats have formally demanded answers from the Pentagon about the crew's welfare and the conditions under which they are serving.

The dispute reflects broader political tensions over the Iran military campaign and its human costs. Critics, primarily Democrats, argue the extended deployment without adequate resupply and mental health support represents a failure of military leadership and a breach of duty of care to service members. The administration contends that the military is properly supporting its personnel and that negative coverage is distorting the reality of life aboard the carrier.

The Lincoln's deployment has become a flashpoint for congressional oversight of the Pentagon under Hegseth, whose tenure has already drawn scrutiny over military readiness and command decisions related to ongoing Middle East operations.

stories.headline: Gun Law in Limbo as DOJ Declines to Appeal Federal Ruling Striking Parts of 1934 National Firearms Act
stories.summary:
The Trump Justice Department has yet to appeal a significant federal court ruling handed down last week that struck down portions of the National Firearms Act of 1934 — one of the country's foundational gun control statutes — leaving the legal landscape for certain regulated firearms in legal limbo. The administration's silence past the expected window for an appeal has drawn alarm from gun control advocates and cautious optimism from Second Amendment groups who believe DOJ may be choosing to let the ruling stand.

The NFA governs the registration, taxation, and transfer of firearms including machine guns, short-barreled rifles, and suppressors. A ruling that parts of it 'can no longer stand' could significantly curtail the federal government's ability to regulate those categories of weapons, affecting millions of existing registrations and the framework for future enforcement.

Gun control organizations argue that failing to appeal represents a deliberate and consequential policy choice by the Trump administration to allow the erosion of longstanding federal firearms law without congressional action. Second Amendment advocates counter that the NFA's restrictions are constitutionally suspect under recent Supreme Court precedent and that the ruling is a legitimate correction.

The DOJ has not publicly explained its decision not to appeal, and it is unclear whether the administration will ultimately challenge the ruling or allow it to take effect. The case adds to a growing body of post-Bruen litigation reshaping federal gun law.

stories.headline: Hurricane Watch Issued for Hawaii's Big Island as Tropical Storm Lala Strengthens in Pacific
stories.summary:
A hurricane watch was issued Thursday for Hawaii's Big Island as Tropical Storm Lala formed in the Pacific Ocean approximately 700 miles east-southeast of the archipelago, with maximum sustained winds of 40 mph. The National Hurricane Center forecasts the storm will strengthen and could approach near-hurricane intensity as it nears the islands, with tropical-storm-force winds and dangerous surf possible beginning late Friday.

Forecasters warned that Lala could deliver 5 to 10 inches of rain across the Hawaiian Islands, with isolated totals of up to 20 inches in some areas. That level of rainfall raises the risk of significant flooding and mudslides, particularly on the Big Island's slopes. A hurricane watch indicates that hurricane conditions are possible and is typically issued 48 hours ahead of the anticipated arrival of tropical-storm-force winds.

A second tropical storm, Hernan, also formed Thursday in the Pacific but was tracking well west of Baja California and posed no immediate threat to land. In the Atlantic, former Tropical Storm Cristobal weakened into a post-tropical remnant low and was not threatening any landmass.

Hawaii is infrequently struck by hurricanes, but when storms do track close to the islands they can cause severe damage due to the terrain's vulnerability to flooding and the state's geographic isolation. Residents of the Big Island were urged to monitor forecasts closely and take preparedness steps ahead of the weekend.

stories.headline: Zambia Holds Presidential Election as Incumbent Seeks Second Term
stories.summary:
Zambians voted Thursday in a presidential and parliamentary election, with more than eight million registered voters casting ballots across the country. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, who won power in 2021 on his sixth attempt, is seeking a second five-year term and is running on a record of debt restructuring, currency stabilization, and infrastructure investment. His main challenger is Brian Mundubile, a former minister under the previous Patriotic Front government.

The election is widely seen as a test of Zambia's standing as one of Africa's more stable democracies, as well as a referendum on Hichilema's economic stewardship. Unemployment and the rising cost of living remain central voter concerns, with some backing the opposition out of frustration with economic hardship despite macroeconomic improvements. Civil society monitors reported mostly orderly voting alongside some procedural delays, and international observers are present.

The contest has been shadowed by political tensions, including a bitter dispute over the unburied remains of former President Edgar Lungu, who died more than a year ago, and Amnesty International's criticism of the government for restricting rights and freedoms ahead of the vote. A candidate must win more than 50 percent of the vote to avoid a runoff.

The outcome carries regional significance as a signal of democratic consolidation or backsliding in southern Africa at a time when several neighboring countries have faced political instability.

stories.headline: Poland Says It Thwarted Russian Plot to Kill American Citizen on NATO Territory
stories.summary:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced Thursday that Polish authorities, working in cooperation with U.S. intelligence services, thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw before it could be carried out. A suspect allegedly recruited by Russia's secret services was detained on August 7. Tusk described it as the first known instance of Russia ordering a killing targeting an American citizen on the soil of a NATO member state.

The targeted individual was described by Polish officials as a U.S. citizen of Ukrainian origin who was 'uncomfortable for the Putin regime,' though further details about the person's identity or activities were not immediately provided. Poland's intelligence oversight minister, Tomasz Siemoniak, confirmed the operation involved close coordination with American counterparts. The Russian Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The disclosure adds to a growing body of reported Russian assassination and sabotage operations in Europe, which Western governments have publicly attributed to Moscow over the past two years. NATO allies have repeatedly raised alarms about Russian hybrid warfare activities, including arson, infrastructure sabotage, and targeted killings, on European soil.

The incident is likely to intensify diplomatic pressure on Russia from both Poland and the broader NATO alliance, and raises questions about the scope of Russian intelligence operations directed at Ukrainian diaspora communities in the West.

stories.headline: Update: Rep. Max Miller's Ex-Wife Files Lawsuit Alleging Nude Image of Toddler Was Posted Online
stories.summary:
Emily Moreno, the ex-wife of Ohio Republican Rep. Max Miller, filed a lawsuit Wednesday alleging that Miller uploaded a nude photograph of their two-year-old daughter to a public online folder. The lawsuit claims Miller provided the image to his attorney, Aaron Minc, as part of materials assembled for the couple's custody dispute. Minc subsequently posted a link to the Dropbox folder on social media, where its contents were viewed more than 400,000 times, according to the filing.

Minc has accepted full personal responsibility for the folder's contents, stating the release of the photograph was 'completely unintentional' and that he alone was responsible for assembling and uploading the materials. Miller denied wrongdoing and accused his former wife and media outlets of perpetuating a false narrative, saying investigations found no evidence he harmed his daughter. The new lawsuit is separate from ongoing domestic abuse allegations Moreno has leveled against Miller, which he also denies.

The controversy has escalated into a broader Republican family feud: Moreno's father, Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio, broke his public silence over the weekend, calling on Miller to resign from Congress and seek 'serious psychological help.' Miller has refused to withdraw from his reelection campaign for Ohio's 7th Congressional District, and missed the deadline to be removed from the GOP ballot.

The Cook Political Report had previously shifted Miller's seat to toss-up status amid the domestic violence allegations. The new lawsuit and the intraparty conflict between two prominent Ohio Republicans further complicates the GOP's prospects in what had been a safe district.

stories.headline: White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt to Depart at End of Month
stories.summary:
President Trump announced Thursday that White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave her post at the end of August, citing her desire to spend more time with her two young children. Trump called her one of his "most trusted aides" and said she will remain involved as a top outside adviser and voice within the Republican Party. No successor has been named.

Leavitt, 28, became the youngest person ever to serve as White House press secretary when she took the role at the start of Trump's second term. She returned from maternity leave last month after welcoming her second child in May. In a statement, she said she could not "be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary."

During her tenure, Leavitt had a combative relationship with much of the press corps. Her office stripped the White House Correspondents' Association of its traditional role organizing the press pool and initially barred the Associated Press over its refusal to adopt the administration's preferred term "Gulf of America." Conservative supporters praised her as a fierce and disciplined defender of the president's agenda.

The departure removes one of the most prominent and recognizable faces of the Trump communications operation. The announcement drew wide coverage across the political spectrum, with 15 outlets reporting the story.

stories.headline: Luigi Mangione Expected to Discuss Plea Deal in Federal Court Friday
stories.summary:
Luigi Mangione, charged in connection with the December 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, is expected to appear in federal court Friday for a hearing at which his defense team and federal prosecutors are anticipated to discuss a possible plea arrangement. Sources involved in the federal case told CBS News that a plea deal is likely to be on the table, though Mangione could change course at any point.

Mangione faces federal stalking charges tied to the killing, which occurred outside a Manhattan hotel and drew intense national attention. A separate state murder trial is currently scheduled to begin next month. The federal hearing comes as both cases move forward on parallel tracks.

The case has generated significant public and political debate, with some commentators framing Mangione as a symbol of public frustration with the health insurance industry, while others condemned the killing unreservedly. Legal analysts note that a federal plea deal, if reached, could affect the trajectory of the state proceedings.

The development represents a material new step in a high-profile case that has been closely watched since Mangione's arrest.

stories.headline: Japan PM Calls Putin's Visit to Disputed Kuril Islands 'Absolutely Unacceptable'
stories.summary:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Thursday sharply condemned Russian President Vladimir Putin's first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, calling it "absolutely unacceptable" and saying the trip "wounds the feelings of the Japanese people." Putin visited Iturup — known in Japan as Etorofu — one of four islands in the southern Kuril chain that Japan has claimed as its "Northern Territories" since the Soviet Union seized and depopulated them at the end of World War Two.

Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also issued a formal protest, stating the islands are "inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law." The two countries have never signed a peace treaty following World War Two, with the island dispute serving as the central obstacle. Japan has imposed sanctions on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine and bilateral relations have remained frozen.

Putin's visit, during which Russian state media showed him sampling fish roe and speaking with local residents, is the highest-profile Russian leadership appearance on the islands. Russia has significantly increased its military presence on the islands over the past decade, and last month Chinese and Russian naval vessels conducted a joint patrol through the Kuril straits.

The provocation marks a new low in Japan-Russia relations and underscores Moscow's intent to assert sovereignty over the territory as its broader confrontation with Western-aligned nations continues.

stories.headline: 3 Dead, Nearly 1 Million Without Power After Severe Storms Strike Midwest
stories.summary:
Severe storms swept through the Midwest on Tuesday and into Wednesday, killing three people and leaving nearly one million electricity customers without power across Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky. A 4-year-old boy was killed when a tree fell on his home in Indiana's Jennings County; a second person died in a suspected weather-related house explosion in Portage, Indiana; and a third death was reported in Roseville, Ohio, where emergency crews could not reach the victim due to widespread road blockages.

Wind gusts exceeding 80 mph were recorded across the region. The National Weather Service confirmed two EF1 tornadoes touched down near Chicago — one in southern Cook County and one in eastern Will County. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine declared a state of emergency as flash flood warnings remained in effect for roughly 16 million people on Wednesday.

In Portage, a city about 30 miles southeast of Chicago, police described the storms as "probably the most severe weather event that any of us can remember." So many trees blocked roads that officers parked a mile away and ran toward the burning home on foot. Utility provider AEP deployed more than 2,000 workers, including crews brought in from other states, to restore power in the Columbus, Ohio area alone.

Sixteen inmates at an Ohio prison were transported to hospitals after a lightning strike during an evening meal period, with one airlifted by medical helicopter. The storm system continued to affect the region Wednesday, compounding the damage from what authorities called a disaster-scale event.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Confirms He Secretly Switched Planes at NATO Summit to Evade Iranian Threat
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday publicly confirmed that he was moved off Air Force One following last month's NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, due to a credible Iranian assassination threat. Trump was hidden inside an airport catering container and transferred to a separate military aircraft while Air Force One was sent aloft as a decoy. The extraordinary security operation was first reported by The Washington Post on Monday.

Trump sought to downplay the unusual nature of the maneuver, telling reporters the Secret Service and military advised him to board a different plane and that he complied. 'I get a lot of threats,' he said, adding he did not ask many questions about the specifics of the danger. He also minimized the risk to White House staff, security personnel, and journalists who remained on Air Force One during the decoy flight.

The confirmation marks a materially new development in the story, as Trump himself is now on record acknowledging the incident for the first time. The episode raises questions about the security protocols surrounding presidential travel and the extent of Iranian threat activity targeting U.S. officials during the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict that began in February.

Thirteen news outlets are covering Trump's confirmation, making it one of the most widely reported stories of the day. The incident underscores both the elevated threat environment facing the administration and the lengths to which the Secret Service is going to protect the president.

stories.headline: DOJ Charges Former SPLC Official Heidi Beirich in Superseding Indictment Against Civil Rights Group
stories.summary:
The Department of Justice on Wednesday charged Heidi Beirich, a former senior official at the Southern Poverty Law Center, in a superseding indictment related to the government's broader criminal case against the Alabama-based nonprofit. Beirich, who previously served as the SPLC's chief financial officer and was widely known as a leading expert on far-right extremism, faces charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and related financial crimes. Prosecutors allege she oversaw payments totaling $4.1 million in donor funds to informants embedded in hate groups, including payments for items such as KKK robes and cross burnings.

The charges are the first brought against an individual in the SPLC case. The DOJ alleges the funds were misrepresented to donors and used in ways that constitute fraud. Beirich's attorney pushed back sharply, stating: 'A free and fair society does not use the justice system to silence its political opponents.'

The SPLC has long been a target of conservative critics who contend the organization is politically biased and misuses its 'hate group' designations against mainstream conservative organizations. Supporters of the SPLC argue the prosecution is an example of the Trump administration weaponizing federal law enforcement against civil society groups that have historically monitored the far right.

Eight outlets are covering the story, which carries significant implications for free speech, nonprofit accountability, and the Justice Department's approach to civil rights organizations under the current administration.

stories.headline: Moderate David Crowley Wins Wisconsin Democratic Gubernatorial Primary, Sets Up Fall Race Against Trump-Backed Tom Tiffany
stories.summary:
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley won Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary on Tuesday, defeating democratic socialist state Rep. Francesca Hong in a razor-thin contest that was not decided until early Wednesday morning. Crowley, who would become Wisconsin's first Black governor if elected, pitched himself as a cross-aisle coalition builder best positioned to win the November general election in the key swing state.

Crowley will face Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, who has voted with President Trump 100 percent of the time, in the November midterm contest. Former Republican Gov. Scott Walker acknowledged Tiffany will need to carefully manage questions about his Trump alignment, saying the congressman must tell voters 'that's not what's on the ballot.' Crowley, for his part, pledged to unite his party's progressive and moderate wings, framing the race as Democrats versus 'a MAGA extremist.'

The primary result reflects broader tensions inside the Democratic Party between its establishment and insurgent progressive wings. Crowley's margin over Hong was less than one percentage point, meaning neither ideological faction can claim a decisive mandate. The outcome mirrors a similarly close Michigan Senate Democratic primary the previous week, where a progressive candidate narrowly defeated a moderate backed by the governor.

With twelve outlets covering the story and Wisconsin having been decided by narrow margins in recent presidential cycles, the governor's race is seen as a bellwether for 2028 White House prospects and a test of which Democratic approach can win back Midwestern swing voters.

stories.headline: Update: Colombia Earthquake Death Toll Reaches 265 as Survivor Pulled Alive After 36 Hours
stories.summary:
The death toll from Colombia's 7.4-magnitude earthquake has risen to at least 265, with 496 people still reported missing, President Abelardo de la Espriella announced Wednesday. The quake, which struck Monday near the village of San José del Palmar in Chocó province, has caused widespread destruction across western Colombia, with the cities of Cali and Pereira sustaining the highest casualties.

In a dramatic rescue Wednesday, a 32-year-old woman named Daniela Largo was pulled alive from the rubble in Pereira after a 10-hour operation, having been trapped under four concrete slabs for 36 hours. Firefighters dug two tunnels to reach her — one from above to provide oxygen and one from below to extract her. President de la Espriella hailed her rescue as 'news which fills us with hope.' Largo's 12-year-old son had been awaiting her rescue at home.

More than 200 people remained trapped in Cali as of Tuesday afternoon, with at least 92 buildings collapsed in Pereira alone. Cali's mayor declared a nighttime curfew and deployed soldiers in the worst-hit areas to ensure rescue operations could proceed safely. More than 100 aftershocks have been recorded since the initial quake.

This update brings a material increase in the confirmed death toll — up from more than 200 in previous coverage — and adds the significant new development of a confirmed survivor rescue deep into the emergency response window.
